UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                         BEFORE THE
                           FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Maryland Office of People’s Counsel

v.                                                                        Docket No. EL26-63-000

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. et al.




                ANSWER OF THE VIRGINIA OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL,
                            DIVISION OF CONSUMER COUNSEL



            Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 the Virginia

Office of the Attorney General, Division of Consumer Counsel (“Virginia Consumer Counsel”)

submits this Answer in response to the Amended Complaint of the Maryland Office of People’s

Counsel (“MDOPC”) against PJM Interconnection, LLC (“PJM”) and certain PJM transmission

owners enumerated in the Amended Complaint. 2

            MDOPC argues that PJM’s cost allocation framework for baseline transmission projects is

unjust and unreasonable because it allocates to Maryland transmission costs associated with data

center load growth in other states. 3 MDOPC proposes the Commission direct PJM to adopt a cost

allocation framework that directly assigns such transmission costs to specific PJM zones or to

specific large load customers. 4

            Virginia Consumer Counsel shares MDOPC’s general concerns about socializing the costs

of an expensive transmission buildout caused primarily by new large load data center customers,

but MDOPC’s proposal to allocate such costs exclusively to the zones in which the large load

customers are located is a blunt instrument that would exacerbate existing inequities. However,

Virginia Consumer Counsel would support exploring mechanisms to directly allocate baseline

transmission costs to cost-causing customers where the facts support such treatment.

                                                 BACKGROUND

           On February 9, 2024, MDOPC filed a protest objecting to Maryland’s share of the costs

for PJM’s 2022 Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) Window 3 Projects and arguing

that Virginia should have been assigned even more costs because Virginia’s tax policies had

encouraged data center development and therefore caused the transmission buildout. 5                       The

Commission rejected MDOPC’s protest on both procedural and substantive grounds. 6

Commissioner Clements in her concurrence pointed out that northern Virginia customers had been

allocated approximately half of the costs while Maryland customers had been allocated only about

ten percent. 7        Commissioner Christie in his concurrence questioned whether Maryland’s

legislatively-mandated closure of fossil fuel generator units had a more direct impact on the need

for new transmission infrastructure than Virginia’s data center tax subsidies. 8

           On May 21, 2026, MDOPC filed the instant Amended Complaint, again proposing to shift

costs of PJM transmission upgrades away from Maryland. 9

                                                    ANSWER

           MDOPC alleges that PJM’s existing hybrid load-ratio share and solutions-based

distribution factor transmission cost allocation methodology is unjustly assigning a

disproportionate amount of data center-driven transmission buildout costs to Maryland

customers. 10 MDOPC repeatedly decries Maryland’s $2 billion share of the costs associated with

PJM’s three recent transmission expansion planning windows. 11 But here some overarching

context is critical: Maryland’s share of those total RTEP costs is less than nine percent. 12 And as

PJM pointed out in response to the 2024 MDOPC Protest, the 2022 Window 3 projects were partly

necessitated due to the cumulative impact of major deactivation requests like Brandon Shores in

Maryland. 13

           Virginia Consumer Counsel shares MDOPC’s general concerns with socializing the costs

of an expensive transmission buildout caused primarily by new large load data center customers. 14

Virginia regulators are already working to address many of the issues MDOPC has identified at

the retail level. The Virginia State Corporation Commission (“Virginia SCC”) has convened

technical conferences on data center load growth and load flexibility. 15 In Dominion Energy


and certain transmission owners to show cause as to why PJM’s existing Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”)
remains just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.9 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. et al., 195
FERC ¶ 61,211 (2026). Virginia Consumer Counsel filed its motion to intervene in that proceeding on July 9, 2026.
See (doc-less) Motion to Intervene of Virginia Consumer Counsel in Docket No. EL26-67.

                                                        3
 Virginia’s (“DEV”) most recent biennial rate case, the Virginia SCC directed DEV to implement

a new large-load GS-5 rate class that includes minimum contract terms, collateral requirements,

and minimum demand charges. 16 The Virginia SCC is also considering approval of DEV’s large

load interconnection queue process standards. 17 Finally, in DEV’s pending transmission rate

adjustment clause proceeding, the Virginia SCC is considering various proposals for direct

allocation of supplemental project transmission costs associated with data centers. 18 Virginia

Consumer Counsel has engaged in all of these proceedings to protect residential and small

commercial ratepayers from shouldering a disproportionate share of costs associated with large

load data centers.

            MDOPC proposes two alternative solutions to the alleged infirmities in PJM’s current

transmission cost allocation methodology: directly charge baseline transmission costs to either (a)

the zones where the large load customers causing the costs are located, or (b) the large load

customers causing the costs. 19

            MDOPC’s direct zonal allocation proposal would jettison PJM’s current data-driven

methodology, which is designed to allocate costs based on commensurate benefits, and replace it

with an unfair binary geography test. MDOPC complains that “Maryland ratepayers are paying

substantially for data center-driven transmission buildout by virtue of geographic proximity, not

cost causation.” 20      But direct zonal allocation would perpetuate precisely the same alleged

                                                        4
 inequity: ratepayers in the charged zone would be expected to fund an even greater share of the

data center-driven transmission buildout merely because of their geographic proximity to the data

centers. At the same time, MDOPC’s direct zonal allocation proposal would seem to absolve all

other zones of any cost responsibility for those transmission upgrades, regardless of whether those

zones caused or benefitted from the infrastructure improvements. This proposal would sever costs

from benefits, enabling free ridership and shifting PJM’s cost allocation framework further away

from cost-benefit alignment.

           MDOPC’s suggestion for direct large load customer assignment is more deserving of

consideration. In DEV’s aforementioned transmission rate adjustment clause proceeding at the

Virginia SCC, there are proposals under consideration to allow – or require – large load customers

to directly pay for at least some portion of the supplemental transmission projects required to serve

them, rather than socializing those costs across the DOM Zone. 21 Questions remain as to the scope

and mechanics of any such direct assignment framework at the state level, as well as whether

action at the federal level may be required, but Virginia Consumer Counsel generally supported

exploring the concept of direct assignment of supplemental project costs to large load customers

in that proceeding. 22 Virginia Consumer Counsel would similarly support exploring direct

assignment of baseline transmission costs to large load customers where the facts support such

treatment.

                                                         5
                                         CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, Virginia Consumer Counsel opposes MDOPC’s proposal to

allocate baseline transmission projects driven by data centers directly to the relevant PJM zones,

but Virginia Consumer Counsel would generally support Commission consideration of direct

assignment of transmission costs to large load data center customers.
